title: FDA warns GLP-1 drugs may pose risk of rare condition that causes vision loss
gist: The FDA will require class-wide GLP-1 labeling (Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, Mounjaro) warning of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare optic-nerve condition causing permanent vision loss, after its own meta-analysis of 126 trials found 10 probable cases on GLP-1s versus five on placebo. Evidence remains mixed and causation unproven; the FDA's guidance is softer than the EMA's.

insights.claim: The FDA will require makers of GLP-1 receptor agonists, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound and Mounjaro, to add label warnings about a potential increased risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), which can cause permanent vision loss.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Class-wide label change is a modest overhang on GLP-1 franchises; watch for prescribing or litigation impact rather than demand collapse.
insights.locator: In a drug safety communication Monday

insights.claim: The FDA's own meta-analysis of 126 trials covering over 130,000 patients identified 15 probable NAION cases: 10 on a GLP-1 drug, five on placebo and none on non-GLP-1 drugs.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Absolute event counts are tiny, implying very low absolute risk even if the signal is real.
insights.locator: In the announcement Monday, the FDA reported

insights.claim: In an FDA retrospective cohort of type 2 diabetes patients from 2019-2024, GLP-1 users showed no increased NAION risk versus SGLT-2 inhibitor users but an increased risk versus DPP-4 inhibitor users.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Comparator-dependent results suggest confounding; the safety signal is not robust across drug classes.
insights.locator: The agency also did a retrospective cohort study

insights.claim: The FDA advises providers to consider discontinuing GLP-1s in patients who develop NAION unless benefits clearly outweigh risk, a more flexible stance than the EMA, which in 2025 recommended stopping semaglutide if NAION is confirmed and estimated risk at up to 1 in 10,000 users.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: US regulators are signaling continued broad GLP-1 use; regulatory divergence limits downside in the largest market.
insights.quote: consider discontinuing the GLP-1 RA in patients who develop NAION, unless the benefits of treatment clearly outweigh the risk.
insights.locator: The FDA's statement has a more flexible recommendation

insights.claim: A 2024 Harvard study in JAMA Ophthalmology found NAION in 8.9 percent of diabetic patients on semaglutide versus 1.8 percent on non-GLP-1 drugs, and 6.7 percent versus 0.8 percent among patients with overweight/obesity, after 36 months.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: This alarming first signal drove regulatory scrutiny despite methodological weaknesses.

insights.claim: The original Harvard GLP-1/NAION study likely suffered selection bias because all patients came from a single referral center handling most regional NAION cases, producing incidence far above the general population and limiting generalizability.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Early safety signals from referral-center data tend to overstate risk; follow-up studies have been mixed.
insights.locator: The study had significant limitations, though.

insights.claim: An electronic health records study of 37.1 million diabetes patients found semaglutide generally not linked to NAION, with increased risk appearing only versus empagliflozin under a narrow case definition.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Large real-world data largely contradicts a strong NAION link, supporting a small absolute risk view.
insights.locator: Another study that used an electronic health records database

insights.claim: NAION's background rate of 2 to 10 per 100,000 people, combined with its risk factors (diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, sleep apnea) being common among GLP-1 patients, makes it hard to establish a causal link.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Confounding by indication means the debate is unlikely to be resolved quickly; expect lingering label and litigation noise.
insights.locator: It's unknown how GLP-1 drugs may cause NAION.

insights.claim: The American Academy of Ophthalmology says any GLP-1/NAION association involves small absolute risk and unproven causation, and that the FDA's class-wide warning extends beyond the evidence, which focuses mostly on semaglutide.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Tirzepatide-based drugs (Zepbound, Mounjaro) carry the label despite limited agent-specific data — a point manufacturers may contest.
insights.quote: NAION remains rare, any increase in absolute risk appears small, and causation has not been established.

insights.claim: The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society recommend shared decision-making on starting, continuing or stopping GLP-1 therapy when NAION develops or risk is elevated.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Specialist guidance favors individualized continuation, limiting discontinuation-driven volume loss.
